o: We must filter rows of `Users` whose `email` satisfies four rules: exactly one `@`, ends with `.com`, the local part (before `@`) uses only alphanumerics and underscores, and the domain part (between `@` and `.com`) contains only letters. In the example, `alice@example.com` and `david@domain.com` pass all checks; `bob_at_example.com` has no `@`, `charlie@example.net` has the wrong TLD, and `eve@invalid` lacks `.com`. Since this is a pure pattern-matching task over strings, a single regular expression captures every rule at once, and we order results by `user_id` ascending.
k: All four validity rules collapse into one regex: ^[A-Za-z0-9_]+@[A-Za-z]+\.com$.
Anchors (^ and $) are essential to reject extra characters or multiple @ symbols.
In MySQL use REGEXP_LIKE (8.0+) or RLIKE; escape the dot so it matches a literal period.

a.i: Each condition maps directly onto a regex component: `[A-Za-z0-9_]+` for the local part, exactly one literal `@`, `[A-Za-z]+` for the letter-only domain, an escaped literal `\.com`, and anchors at both ends guarantee nothing extra appears (which also enforces 'exactly one @'). One WHERE clause plus ORDER BY solves the problem.

c.python:
-- Database problem: solution is a single SQL query.
SELECT user_id, email
FROM Users
WHERE REGEXP_LIKE(email, '^[A-Za-z0-9_]+@[A-Za-z]+\\.com$')
ORDER BY user_id;

a.t: O(n * m) where n is the number of rows and m is average email length, since each email is scanned once by the regex engine.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the output.

w: Use the regex approach — it is the idiomatic one-liner interviewers expect for this problem. Common pitfalls: forgetting to escape the dot in `.com` (an unescaped dot would match any character), omitting anchors (allowing strings like `x@@y.com` or trailing junk), using `+` vs `*` incorrectly (empty local part or empty domain must be rejected), and forgetting ORDER BY. Edge cases include emails with digits/underscores in the local part (valid) and digits in the domain (invalid). A likely follow-up asks for the same validation without regex — then split on `@`, verify there are exactly two pieces, check each piece character by character, and confirm the domain ends with the literal suffix `.com`.
